clue.text: Steady young fellows — take a bit of control when up and going

definitions.text: take a bit of control when up and going
definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what these grooms do: they handle a horse by its bit when it is saddled and moving

parts.note: steady and stable both mean firm and not wobbling
lads are boys or young men

explanation.surface: Dependable youths are told to take charge once they are up and about.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bit' is the metal bar in a horse's mouth, and 'up' means mounted. Stable lads are the grooms who look after racehorses.
explanation.definitionFit: Grooms at a racing yard ride out and lead horses, controlling them by the bit in the mouth.

clue.text: A boom is on in part of Sicily

indicators.note: one piece is put inside another, as the word says
only a portion of the island's name is used, its opening letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something explosive is happening on the island.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'A boom is' wants an adjective: a bang made when an aircraft breaks the sound barrier is described this way. 'part of' takes the first three letters of the island's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Supersonic aircraft make a sonic boom, so such a bang is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Solitary woman who's weighed from bed?

definitions.text: Solitary woman who's weighed from bed?

parts.words: Solitary woman who's weighed from bed?
parts.note: a female recluse, read as a ship's hook that is weighed, raised, from the sea bed

explanation.surface: A lonely woman being weighed as she gets out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: To weigh anchor is to haul it up from the sea bed; an anchoress is a woman religious recluse.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchoress was a woman who withdrew from the world to live enclosed as a religious hermit.

clue.text: Left and right about your head, it's crazily he plays

indicators.note: the first pair of letters are placed around another letter
only the opening letter of the following word is used
the letters of the following word are scrambled

explanation.surface: A mad musician performs with his head between left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps left and right round the head of 'your'; 'crazily' scrambles the letters of "it's", the apostrophe giving no letter. A lyrist plays the lyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyrist is a player on the lyre, or a lyric poet.

parts.note: the French stew is set against a famous English stew named after its home county, a hotpot

explanation.surface: Asking where England's version of the French stew comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancashire hotpot is a lamb and potato stew from the north-west English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The English stew equivalent to pot-au-feu is the hotpot that takes this county's name.

parts.note: gull read not as a seabird but as a person fooled, who has no wings

explanation.surface: A seabird that cannot fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gull' looks like the bird; as a verb it means to trick, and as a noun someone easily tricked.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe is someone easily deceived, which is what a gull means as a noun.

indicators.note: to keep something in is to hold it inside, so one word goes within the other here
completes the phrase 'keep ... in', telling us the second word sits inside the first

parts.note: taken as written
mum and ma are both words for mother

explanation.surface: An exclamation urging someone to stay quiet, addressed to a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep mum' looks like the idiom for staying silent, but here 'mum' is mother, kept inside the exclamation. An amah is a nurse or maid in parts of Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: In South and East Asia an amah is a children's nursemaid or wet nurse.

parts.note: one who produces, but read as someone who insists, forcing people to do things ('I'll make you')

explanation.surface: A demanding film or theatre producer.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a producer also suits someone who makes others act, as in 'make him do it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A creator or manufacturer is a producer; to make someone do something is to insist they do it.

clue.text: "Creatures that… teach the act of order to a peopled kingdom"

definitions.text: "Creatures that… teach the act of order to a peopled kingdom"

parts.words: "Creatures that… teach the act of order to a peopled kingdom"
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's Henry V, where the Archbishop of Canterbury praises the order of a hive

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean line about creatures that model order for a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry V, Act 1 Scene 2: 'for so work the honey-bees, Creatures that by a rule in nature teach The act of order to a peopled kingdom.'
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare uses the hive insects as a model of an orderly state.

clue.text: One of four that support the rest and won't split

definitions.text: One of four that support the rest and won't split

parts.words: One of four that support the rest and won't split
parts.note: an upright at a bed's corner holds up the sleeper's rest, and secrets told 'between you and me and the' upright are kept

explanation.surface: A loyal member of a group of four who props up the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' is sleep, not the remainder; 'won't split' refers to the saying 'between you and me and the bedpost', meaning in confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-poster bed stands on four such posts, which hold up the sleeper.

clue.text: In the forenoon I certainly am more agreeable

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of words that follows this word

explanation.surface: Someone admits they are pleasanter company in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' tells you the answer is tucked inside 'forenooN I CERtainly'; 'am' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nicer is pleasanter, kinder or more pleasing than something else.

clue.text: Little drink for a young member of the family?

parts.note: a nipper is a small child, a youngster
kin means relatives, family members

explanation.surface: A small tot of something for a child in the family.
explanation.walkthrough: A nipper is British slang for a small child, and kin are relatives. A nipperkin is an old word for a small measure of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A nipperkin is an archaic small vessel or measure of liquor, about half a pint or less.

clue.text: Tennyson expected to over the head of the goalie?

definitions.text: over the head of the goalie

explanation.surface: A poet's expectation is linked to something above a goalkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem 'Crossing the Bar' is about death, expected as a crossing of the sandbar at sea; the goal's top bar sits above the goalkeeper's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson anticipated he would cross the bar at death; the horizontal goal beam runs above the keeper.

explanation.surface: A plant, perhaps galloping off in a hurry on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurry is a small weedy plant of the pink family. The second reading coins an adjective: a rider in haste is all spurs and hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurry is a low-growing herb of fields; a hurried rider is spurring the horse, hence the coined adjective.

parts.note: a jack-in-the-box leaps up on a coiled spring, and this tiny insect jumps by flicking a forked tail

explanation.surface: Asking about a bug that pops up like the toy.
explanation.walkthrough: These tiny wingless creatures leap by releasing a tail-like organ held under the body.
explanation.definitionFit: These small soil insects jump by means of a forked appendage folded under the abdomen.

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, as the word says

parts.note: a company of males is men
one is the Roman numeral I; the 's is the verb 'is'

explanation.surface: How a person carries themselves among other men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' looks like part of 'One's bearing', but it is the definition; I goes inside MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Mien is a person's look, manner or bearing.

parts.note: handlebar is a style of facial hair with upturned ends, here imagined flying out in the wind

explanation.surface: A bicycle part sailing through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handlebar' seems to be a bicycle part, but a handlebar is a wide upper-lip growth with curled ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A handlebar is a broad upper-lip growth whose ends curl up, said to fly out.

clue.text: Mainly keeping a sharp look ahead, while looking round behind

definitions.text: Mainly keeping a sharp look ahead, while looking round behind

parts.words: Mainly keeping a sharp look ahead, while looking round behind
parts.note: 'Mainly' means on the main, the sea: a vessel keeps a sharp lookout ahead, and a rounded figure behind gives a good form, so the whole means neat and in good order

explanation.surface: Someone watching keenly in front while also glancing over their shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as SHIP, a vessel on the 'main' or ocean keeping lookout ahead, and SHAPE, the shapely round behind; together they mean tidy and in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipshape means neat and orderly, as a well-run vessel must be.

clue.text: Trouble, got my share of it, dear love

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble, as in 'much ado about nothing'
a ration is one person's allotted share

explanation.surface: A lover complains about the trouble and the portion they were given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got' is a link between the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoration is deep, devoted love.

clue.text: How you feel when you're cornered

definitions.text: How you feel when you're cornered

parts.words: How you feel when you're cornered
parts.note: cornered read literally as having corners, so the feeling is bony and sharp-edged

explanation.surface: Asking about the emotions of someone trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cornered' suggests trapped, but read literally it means having corners.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with sharp corners is described with this adjective.

explanation.surface: A spiny animal is likened to a biblical patriarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Abram (later Abraham) came from Ur of the Chaldees, so he was 'Ur's son'. The urson is the North American porcupine.
explanation.definitionFit: The urson is the Canadian porcupine; Abram was born in Ur, so a son of that city.

clue.text: Beribboned Academician seen in sun and showers

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
beribboned means decked in ribbons, that is, in bows

explanation.surface: A decorated painter turns up in mixed weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beribboned' is read as 'in bows', placed after RA. RA is the British title for a member of the Royal Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcs of colour appear when sunlight shines through falling rain.

parts.note: she is the pronoun for that girl
wed means married

explanation.surface: A woman's marriage is confirmed.
explanation.walkthrough: Shewed is an old spelling of showed.
explanation.definitionFit: To show something is to demonstrate or prove it; shewed is the archaic past tense.

parts.note: china here is crockery, and the storm is the one in the idiom about a fuss over nothing taking place in a small cup

explanation.surface: A country at the heart of a political tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but it is porcelain; a 'storm in a teacup' is a great fuss about something trivial.
explanation.definitionFit: A china cup for drinking is where the proverbial small storm takes place.

clue.text: Wishful strange dream of Venus de Milo ?

definitions.text: Wishful strange dream of Venus de Milo

indicators.note: the letters of the next word are rearranged, made strange

explanation.surface: The armless statue has a curious, longing dream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges DREAM. The Venus de Milo statue has lost both arms, so she might dream of having them.
explanation.definitionFit: Having arms is what the armless statue would wish for.

explanation.surface: Clever people are assaulted with cutlery.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is the top of a boiled egg, broken into with a spoon at breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Highbrows are called this informally; boiled eggs have their tops cracked open with spoons.

parts.note: read not as the Australian state but as a queen's land from ancient times, the realm of a biblical queen

explanation.surface: An earlier name for an Australian state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queensland' looks like the Australian state, but it is the land of the Queen of Sheba, who visited Solomon.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical queen who visited Solomon ruled this ancient kingdom.

parts.note: Thomas Hardy's novel about an obscure stonemason, title character of 'the Obscure'

explanation.surface: A tough but little-known character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective, but it is Thomas Hardy, whose last novel is 'Jude the Obscure'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Hardy's 1895 novel is called the Obscure.

clue.text: A plant perhaps for contrary Mary's garden

definitions.text: A plant perhaps for contrary Mary's garden

parts.words: A plant perhaps for contrary Mary's garden
parts.note: the nursery rhyme garden grows silver bells, and this is the bellflower genus

explanation.surface: A suggestion of what to grow in the nursery rhyme garden.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary', the garden grows 'silver bells and cockle shells'; campanula is Latin for little bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Campanulas are bellflowers, so they suit a garden of silver bells.

indicators.note: the words that follow are put wrong, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone protests whenever they are in the wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' rearranges WHEN I.
explanation.definitionFit: To whine is to complain in a peevish, drawn-out way.

parts.note: two ways are two compass directions, here east and north, E and N
D is the abbreviation for an old penny (Latin denarius), and the 's adds its S

explanation.surface: What a reversible coin is for.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for a penny in Britain's old pounds, shillings and pence money.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends are aims or goals, as in 'the end justifies the means'.

clue.text: She's an eyeful — makes pupils expansive

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman makes the students open up.
explanation.walkthrough: Italian bella donna means beautiful lady; the plant gives atropine, once used to widen the pupils of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian phrase means a lovely woman; deadly nightshade extract dilates the pupils.
